studyPaths.name: Kotlin execution and core semantics
studyPaths.description: The first complete group: JVM API shape, properties, control flow, functions, classes, construction, visibility, equality, and safe initialization. Basic syntax stays searchable off the path.

scenario.title: Review a Kotlin cache policy for Java callers
scenario.context: A Java service calls a Kotlin cache policy. The complete Policy.kt and PolicyClient.java example is in Initialization order and safe construction. Start with a Policy whose base constructor records base and whose init block records init. Its final title is ready. Two separately allocated RequestKey values both have primary-constructor id 7; their body property notes differ.

stages.prompt: The safe BasePolicy receives title directly as a constructor argument. Predict the trace after constructing Policy. A proposed rewrite makes title open and reads it through an override in the base init block: can you promise that this reads ready?
stages.feedback: Safe construction records base,init. The proposed virtual read can reach derived state before it is initialized. The Kotlin specification makes an early property read unspecified; a particular JVM zero/null observation is not a portable guarantee. Pass the needed input directly and keep construction-time behavior final.
stages.nextConstraint: Construction is now safe. The cache compares the two RequestKey instances with ==; note remains a body property.

stages.prompt: Predict left == right and left === right. Will different notes separate these keys? Explain the effect of moving a mutable note into the primary constructor before using the objects as hash keys.
stages.feedback: Equality is true because generated data-class equality uses the primary-constructor id; identity is false because these are distinct allocations. The body notes are ignored. Moving note into the constructor includes it in equality and hashCode; mutating it while used as a key can invalidate lookup assumptions.
stages.nextConstraint: ID-only equality is deliberate. The decision expression chooses reuse for equal keys and reload otherwise, inside try with cleanup in finally.

stages.prompt: The try block ends with if (left == right) reuse else reload. Finally appends cleanup to the trace and ends with the string ignored. Which decision is returned, and what is the complete trace? What changes if cleanup throws?
stages.feedback: The decision is reuse and the trace is base,init,cleanup. A normally completing finally does not supply the try result. If cleanup throws, the function fails instead of returning reuse and can mask an earlier failure.
stages.nextConstraint: Java must call the top-level decide function in Policy.kt and read Policy.title through the generated API.

stages.prompt: Name the Java entry point for decide(left, right) and the title accessor. State the expected complete output of the example, then propose tests and API constraints that preserve this behavior during a refactor.
stages.feedback: Java calls PolicyKt.decide(left, right) and policy.getTitle(). The verified example prints base,init,cleanup:reuse:true:false:ready. Preserve or intentionally version the facade and accessor, compile a real Java consumer, assert output, and keep equality-relevant state stable. The language-level ordering and equality contracts are distinct from the chosen JVM API shape.
stages.nextConstraint: Review construction, equality, control flow, and JVM exposure as one API contract before marking the group scenario-ready.

debrief.connections: Construction establishes the state that accessors expose; the key's equality contract chooses the control-flow branch; finally determines whether that result reaches the caller; generated facade and accessor methods define how Java reaches the Kotlin behavior.
debrief.tradeOffs: Constructor inputs make dependencies explicit. ID-only equality intentionally ignores notes; including mutable notes broadens equality but makes hashed keys fragile. Expression form keeps the decision local, while effectful cleanup can obscure failure. Stable Java API names add compatibility obligations.
rubric: Traces base before derived initialization and rejects constructor-time virtual reads without promising unspecified values.
Predicts value equality true and identity false, identifies excluded body properties, and explains stable hashing.
Predicts reuse after normal cleanup and explains abrupt completion from finally.
Names PolicyKt.decide and getTitle, predicts the complete output, and proposes a real Java consumer test.
Connects the decisions and distinguishes language guarantees, documented JVM API mapping, and implementation observations.

studyPaths.name: Kotlin type system and null safety
studyPaths.description: Reason from Kotlin's nullable, flow-sensitive, top, bottom, and unit types, then normalize uncertain Java values at the boundary.

scenario.title: Make an uncertain Java customer boundary safe
scenario.context: A Kotlin service calls the unannotated Java LegacyCustomerApi.lookup method. The method returns Object, may return null, and may return a value of the wrong runtime type. Kotlin must produce a non-blank display label or reject the invalid value without masking uncertainty behind !!. The complete runnable example is in the Nothing lesson.

stages.prompt: What uncertainty enters Kotlin from the unannotated Java Object return? Predict the risk of assigning it directly to non-null Any and explain the first type you would write at the boundary.
stages.feedback: The Java result enters as the platform type Any!. Assigning a returned null directly to Any can compile and fail at the generated null check. Normalize immediately as Any? so both absence and the unknown runtime subtype remain explicit.
stages.nextConstraint: The normalized value is Any?. Null means no public name, String is the only accepted payload, and every other runtime type is an upstream contract violation.

stages.prompt: Design the when branches for Any?. Where do smart casts apply, what does the null branch produce, and why does the invalid branch type-check when it calls a function returning Nothing?
stages.feedback: Handle null with the explicit Anonymous fallback, use is String so the matching branch smart-casts the stable subject, and send the else branch to reject(...): Nothing. Nothing is a subtype of every result type, so that branch can abort while the whole when still has type String.
stages.nextConstraint: A present String may contain surrounding whitespace or become empty after trimming. The service also needs an audit side effect whose result is deliberately ignored.

stages.prompt: Choose between a safe-call chain, an explicit check, Elvis handling, and !! for the String branch. Also state the type and meaning of the audit function's return.
stages.feedback: Trim the already smart-cast String and use takeIf plus Elvis to turn blank text into Anonymous. An explicit check would be equally honest when distinct branches need different effects. !! is unjustified because absence is known domain data, not an impossible state. The audit function returns Unit: one ordinary value that makes the effectful function usable in Kotlin's expression and generic type system.
stages.nextConstraint: The boundary now produces Ada for text, Anonymous for null or blank text, and a deliberate IllegalArgumentException for any other runtime type.

stages.prompt: Defend the completed boundary design and its tests. Under what stronger invariant, if any, could !! be justified, and which Kotlin 2.4 Java-boundary changes must a migration review consider?
stages.feedback: Keep Any? at the uncertain edge, test text, null, blank, and wrong-type cases, and expose only the normalized String downstream. !! is defensible only when a separately enforced invariant proves non-null and an immediate NullPointerException is the intended invariant failure. Kotlin 2.4 also rejects unsafe flexible nullable type arguments, enforces Jakarta nullability annotations, and tightens non-abstract Java sealed-class exhaustiveness; annotation target and metadata changes matter when recompiling boundary declarations.
stages.nextConstraint: Review the platform assumption, flow proof, fallback, exceptional branch, Unit effect, and failure policy as one boundary contract before marking the group scenario-ready.

debrief.connections: The platform type marks an uncertain Java contract; Any? preserves both nullability and runtime-type uncertainty; smart casts refine a stable value after checks; Elvis selects the blank-name policy; Nothing makes rejection compose with the String result; Unit names the audit effect; and !! remains an explicit invariant assertion rather than a conversion strategy.
debrief.tradeOffs: Normalizing at the edge adds handling code but confines uncertainty. A fallback preserves availability but must match the domain meaning of absence. Rejecting unexpected runtime types fails early with context. !! is shorter only by discarding an uncertainty the boundary actually has.
rubric: Identifies Any! as a platform type, predicts the non-null assignment risk, and normalizes it to Any? at the Java boundary.
Uses a stable when subject and explains the String smart cast, the null fallback, and the invalid-type branch.
Explains why Nothing composes with a String result and why Unit represents the completed audit effect.
Chooses safe calls, Elvis, or explicit checks according to the policy and rejects unjustified !! usage.
Tests every boundary outcome and labels Kotlin 2.4-specific Java interoperability behavior instead of presenting it as timeless.

studyPaths.name: Kotlin domain modeling
studyPaths.description: Choose deliberately among Kotlin's data, closed-state, singleton, wrapper, delegation, and immutability constructs while preserving a usable JVM API.

scenario.title: Design a durable order model for Kotlin and Java
scenario.context: A Kotlin order library serves Kotlin code and a Java checkout service. Orders need validated IDs, draft/submitted/rejected states with different payloads, a small priority classification, snapshot tags, a replaceable currency policy, and a Java-friendly factory. The complete runnable mixed Kotlin/Java model is in Immutability, aliases, and stable invariants.

stages.prompt: Choose representations for OrderId and Order itself. Which properties define order equality, what does copy promise, and where could boxing or Java interop change the runtime shape?
stages.feedback: Use a value class when the single String ID invariant and Kotlin type distinction justify its representation caveats. Use a data class only if its primary-constructor properties honestly define order value equality. Its copy is shallow; broad, nullable, interface, and generic value-class uses can box, and Java-facing value-class APIs require separate design.
stages.nextConstraint: An order can be draft, submitted with a total, or rejected with a reason. Priority is standard or express and carries no per-order payload.

stages.prompt: Choose between enums, nullable fields, and a sealed hierarchy for state and priority. Show how a consumer gets exhaustiveness feedback when a new order state is added.
stages.feedback: Use sealed payload variants for the order state so invalid field combinations are unrepresentable, and an enum for the fixed singleton priority values. An exhaustive subject-based when without else forces compiled consumers to handle a new relevant variant.
stages.nextConstraint: Construction must accept caller-owned mutable tags, expose no mutation path, and provide a Java-friendly create or submit entry point.

stages.prompt: Design tag ownership and the companion factory. Explain why val plus List is insufficient by itself and name the Java call with and without @JvmStatic.
stages.feedback: Use an ordinary class with a private constructor and store an unmodifiable snapshot; a data class would expose a generated copy path that accepts another arbitrary List. val prevents reassignment and Kotlin List removes writes through that view but neither alone revokes aliases or prevents Java from calling mutators on a mutable implementation. The mixed example tests both the retained input and Java getter. A String-taking @JvmStatic bridge permits Order.submit without exposing the mangled value-class signature.
stages.nextConstraint: Checkout needs a default USD policy, but tests and other regions must substitute another implementation without inheritance or global mutation.

stages.prompt: Choose an object and delegation design for currency policy, then defend the complete model against identity, copying, boxing, initialization, exhaustiveness, and Java API regressions.
stages.feedback: A stateless object can provide the default strategy, while a checkout wrapper uses interface delegation and overrides only policy it owns. Test generated data-class equality and shallow-copy assumptions, exhaustive state handling, value-class boxing boundaries, object and companion initialization expectations, mutable-input snapshots, and the real Java factory call.
stages.nextConstraint: Review the closed state space, ownership boundaries, generated members, representation choices, and JVM surface as one evolving domain contract before marking the scenario-ready state.

debrief.connections: The closed state space determines exhaustive behavior; primary-constructor properties determine generated equality and shallow copy; the value class separates IDs while introducing boxing and JVM-boundary choices; snapshots protect immutability; objects provide singleton strategies; delegation composes policy; and companion annotations determine the Java call shape.
debrief.tradeOffs: Stronger types and closed variants reject invalid states but increase migration coordination. Generated members reduce boilerplate while making constructor membership contractual. Snapshots allocate to clarify ownership. Static bridges improve Java ergonomics while enlarging the binary API. Delegation reduces forwarding code but requires deliberate interception boundaries.
rubric: Chooses data or ordinary classes from equality, identity, and copying semantics rather than brevity.
Separates enum singleton choices from sealed payload variants and preserves exhaustive maintenance feedback.
Explains value-class boxing and Java-facing shape without promising universal allocation removal.
Distinguishes val, read-only views, and immutable snapshots and identifies shallow-copy aliases.
Uses objects, companions, and delegation with explicit initialization, interception, and Java API tests.

studyPaths.name: Kotlin collections and sequences
studyPaths.description: Choose collection capabilities, ownership, transformations, grouping, and eager or lazy evaluation from semantics and cost.

scenario.title: Choose a collection pipeline for a bounded report
scenario.context: A reporting source accepts and retains a caller-owned mutable batch of immutable Sale values, then produces a report later. It must retain a stable structural snapshot, skip refunds, normalize region names, stop after three accepted sales, and return counts per region. The complete runnable example is in Sequences, evaluation, and pipeline cost.

stages.prompt: The caller may mutate its MutableList after the source accepts it but before a later report runs. Is storing it as List enough? Choose between a live read-only view and a snapshot, and state what remains shared after a shallow copy.
stages.feedback: List restricts writes through one reference but does not revoke the caller's mutable alias. Copy when the source accepts the input because a later report requires the accepted batch to remain stable. The immutable Sale values may safely be shared; mutable elements would require a deeper ownership policy.
stages.nextConstraint: The snapshot may contain hundreds of thousands of sales. Enrichment is expensive, refunds do not count, and only the first three accepted sales belong in this report.

stages.prompt: Compare an eager filter/map/take chain with a sequence or explicit loop. Predict which sales the sequence example inspects and where work begins.
stages.feedback: The eager collection transformations complete their passes before take can limit their work. The sequence starts only at the terminal aggregation, interleaves per-element operations, and stops after the third accepted sale: it inspects four inputs because the second is refunded. A loop could express the same bound with explicit state.
stages.nextConstraint: The report needs counts per normalized region, not member lists, and its output order must be stable for serialization.

stages.prompt: Choose between groupBy, associateBy, and groupingBy().eachCount(). Explain retained data, duplicate regions, terminal behavior, and ordering.
stages.feedback: groupingBy().eachCount() retains a count per region and is terminal, so it drives the sequence. groupBy would also retain lists of sales or regions that the result does not need. associateBy would overwrite duplicate regions. Sort the result explicitly at the serialization boundary rather than relying on observed map iteration order.
stages.nextConstraint: A reviewer asks whether replacing the eager chain with a sequence proves the service is faster and whether the returned report can be reused safely.

stages.prompt: Defend the ownership and evaluation design, state what the deterministic example proves, and identify measurements or changed constraints that could favor an eager chain or loop.
stages.feedback: The snapshot protects structural ownership between acceptance and later reporting, and the sequence avoids processing the fifth snapshot element; the terminal count materializes a reusable map. The example proves evaluation order, inspected elements, independence from the cleared input alias, and the semantic result—not an exact allocation count or universal speedup. Small inputs, cheap operations, all-matching data, repeated consumption, or stateful sorting may favor eager collections or a loop; benchmark representative workloads.
stages.nextConstraint: Review ownership, shallow element sharing, eager versus lazy traversal, terminal aggregation, ordering, and measured cost as one design before marking the scenario-ready state.

debrief.connections: The read-only interface controls capabilities while the snapshot establishes structural ownership; transformation choice controls traversal and intermediate results; sequence demand controls evaluation order and early termination; and terminal grouping materializes the reusable report.
debrief.tradeOffs: Copying clarifies ownership at an allocation cost. Eager operations are simple and reusable but can perform avoidable passes. Sequences may avoid work and intermediate collections but add per-element machinery and delayed execution. Direct aggregation retains less data than member groups, while explicit sorting pays for a stable external order.
rubric: Distinguishes a read-only view from a stable snapshot and identifies shallowly shared elements.
Predicts eager operation-by-operation traversal and lazy element-by-element traversal through terminal demand.
Chooses groupingBy().eachCount() from the required result and rejects duplicate-overwriting associateBy.
Identifies the four inspected inputs, the skipped fifth input, and the explicitly sorted output without overclaiming allocation details.
Rejects automatic performance claims and names workload changes and measurements that could change the choice.

studyPaths.name: Kotlin functions and idioms
studyPaths.description: Design readable Kotlin APIs with lambdas, extensions, receivers, scope functions, and inline or reified capabilities without hiding intent.

scenario.title: Design and defend a readable higher-order API
scenario.context: An event library serves Kotlin and Java applications. Callers need the first event payload of a requested runtime type and kind that satisfies a policy. The Kotlin API may use extensions, a receiver lambda, inline code, and a reified type; Java still needs an honest callable core. The complete runnable Kotlin design is in Inline control flow and reified type parameters.

stages.prompt: Design the predicate boundary. Should it be a plain function type, receiver function type, or named functional interface? State when and how often it runs, what happens on failure, and what Java callers need.
stages.feedback: A receiver predicate such as T.() -> Boolean is readable when payload members are its sole focus; an explicit (T) -> Boolean is better when the value name or additional receivers matter. The query must document encounter order, first-match termination, exception propagation, and invocation only for payloads of the requested type and kind. A Java boundary should expose a class token plus a Java-friendly functional interface or another deliberate overload rather than relying on a reified-only entry point.
stages.nextConstraint: Kind normalization is useful outside the query, but Event is a library model whose virtual members cannot be changed. The team proposes extension syntax.

stages.prompt: Decide whether kind normalization and event querying deserve extensions. Explain static resolution, identify every receiver in the proposed query, and remove any receiver syntax that falsely suggests ownership or becomes ambiguous.
stages.feedback: A focused String.normalizedKind extension is honest because the String is the primary input and the operation needs no hidden state. An Iterable<Event> query extension can be discoverable, but remains a statically resolved helper rather than a new virtual collection member. Inside a receiver predicate, T is the lambda receiver while the iterable is the extension receiver of the outer function; name event and payload locals explicitly so those roles do not compete. Use an ordinary service when dependencies or multiple peer inputs grow.
stages.nextConstraint: The Kotlin call should avoid an explicit class token. A reviewer proposes inline plus reified T and says this will make the query faster.

stages.prompt: Evaluate inline and reified T. Separate source control-flow effects, emitted bytecode, performance evidence, type-erasure limits, binary/API costs, and the Java alternative.
stages.feedback: Inline plus reified T permits the runtime payload check without a token and may inline the predicate at Kotlin call sites. It can duplicate bytecode, couples compiled callers to public inline implementation, does not preserve arbitrary nested generic arguments, and is not automatically faster. Non-local returns are possible only for eligible inline lambda use; choose crossinline or noinline if invocation or storage requires them. Keep or expose a token-based non-inline core for Java and benchmark only if query cost matters.
stages.nextConstraint: An implementation chains let, run, apply, and also around the query because they are considered idiomatic, but reviewers cannot tell which value each step returns.

stages.prompt: Rewrite and defend the complete API. Explain any remaining scope function by receiver and result behavior, predict the checked example, and propose tests for resolution, lambda invocation, control flow, type access, Java use, and readability regressions.
stages.feedback: Keep direct locals and firstNotNullOfOrNull because the phases and returned nullable payload are clearer than a mixed scope-function chain; takeIf remains a small predicate-to-value operation. The example skips the charge kind and the legacy String payload, then returns the 75-cent refunded Payment and prints refund:75. Test static extension resolution separately, predicate call count and order, no-match and thrown-predicate behavior, non-local versus labeled returns, supported reified checks and erased nested types, a real Java token-based call, and code review criteria for receiver ambiguity and hidden effects.
stages.nextConstraint: Review the function contract, receiver ownership, static resolution, returned values, inline bytecode and control flow, reified limits, and cross-language surface as one API before marking the scenario-ready state.

debrief.connections: The higher-order contract owns predicate timing; extension syntax makes the primary inputs discoverable without changing their classes; explicit locals control receiver ambiguity; scope-function selection follows receiver and result needs; inline enables specific control flow and call-site generation; and reification supplies Kotlin runtime type access while a token-based core preserves Java reachability.
debrief.tradeOffs: A receiver lambda is concise when one object is central but can hide which receiver wins. Extensions improve Kotlin fluency while remaining static helpers. Scope functions improve locality only while value flow stays obvious. Inline and reified syntax can remove a token for Kotlin callers at the cost of duplicated bytecode, binary coupling, and a separate Java design. Clear ordinary code is preferable to stacking idioms.
rubric: Defines predicate timing, order, result, exception, and capture behavior instead of stopping at the function type.
Explains static extension resolution and distinguishes extension, dispatch, and lambda receivers.
Chooses scope functions from receiver and return-value semantics and removes them when locals are clearer.
Separates inline source semantics, bytecode consequences, performance evidence, API evolution, and non-local-return constraints.
Uses reified access within erasure limits, supplies a Java-facing alternative, and defends the complete API with behavioral and readability tests.

studyPaths.name: Kotlin generics and abstraction
studyPaths.description: Design type-safe Kotlin APIs by separating constraints, substitutability, projected capabilities, and runtime type evidence.

scenario.title: Design and defend a type-safe variant API
scenario.context: A message library returns either a typed success payload or a failure and must let broad consumers handle narrower payloads. One diagnostic boundary also receives values whose generic arguments are unknown at runtime. The complete runnable design is in Erased generic runtime types.

stages.prompt: Choose the type parameters and bounds for comparing and identifying messages. Which operations should the generic body be allowed to use, and why should unrelated capabilities stay out of the bound?
stages.feedback: Give T only the bounds required by the implementation, using a where clause when it needs both identity and comparison. A bound is a compile-time capability contract, not proof of a concrete runtime type. Extra bounds reject useful callers and couple the abstraction to operations it does not own.
stages.nextConstraint: A success produces its payload, a failure has no payload, and a renderer consumes values. The API must accept Result<Invoice> where Result<Any> is expected and a Renderer<Any> where Renderer<Invoice> is needed.

stages.prompt: Place in or out on the result and renderer declarations. Explain each substitution and identify any method that would make the declaration unsafe.
stages.feedback: Result<out T> is covariant because clients only receive T, so Result<Invoice> is substitutable for Result<Any>. Renderer<in T> is contravariant because it only accepts T, so Renderer<Any> can render an Invoice. Adding a T-consuming method to Result or a T-producing method to Renderer violates those promises; invariance is correct when a type genuinely does both.
stages.nextConstraint: An invariant mutable buffer must be copied from a narrow element type into a broad one, and an inspection endpoint receives a container whose argument is unknown.

stages.prompt: Design the buffer parameters with use-site projections and explain exactly what may be read or written. Then explain what Container<*> permits without guessing its hidden argument.
stages.feedback: Read the source through out T and write the destination through in T. These are restricted views of invariant containers, not declarations that permanently change the container type. A star projection safely represents an unknown argument: reads use its upper bound and writes requiring that unknown type are unavailable. It resembles an unbounded Java wildcard, not an unsafe Java raw type.
stages.nextConstraint: Diagnostics now ask whether an arbitrary value is Result<Invoice>, while Kotlin callers want a concise typed filter and Java callers will later need a deliberate interop surface.

stages.prompt: State which checks survive erasure, where an unchecked cast would lie, what reified T can check, and how you would test and expose the complete API across the later Java boundary.
stages.feedback: Runtime code may check Result<*> or List<*>, not generally Result<Invoice> or List<String>. An unchecked cast shifts responsibility to an invariant that must be validated at the boundary. Reified T can check each element against a runtime-available T at an inline call site, but nested arguments remain erased. Test covariance, contravariance, projected restrictions, star reads, failures, erased checks, and reified element checks; review generated Java wildcards separately in the interoperability group.
stages.nextConstraint: Review compile-time substitutability, available operations, runtime type evidence, and future Java API shape as four separate parts of the variant contract before marking the scenario-ready state.

debrief.connections: Generic bounds grant compile-time operations; declaration-site variance defines compile-time substitutability for producer and consumer abstractions; use-site and star projections restrict capabilities when the declaration is invariant or unknown; type erasure limits runtime questions; and reification supplies selected call-site evidence without restoring nested arguments.
debrief.tradeOffs: Narrow bounds admit more callers but expose fewer operations. Variance improves substitution while forbidding unsafe member positions. Projections make one use safe but deliberately reduce operations. Star projections preserve uncertainty, unchecked casts hide it, and reified conveniences trade an inline Kotlin-only surface for limited runtime checks. Java wildcard shape remains a separate API review.
rubric: Uses only necessary generic bounds and distinguishes them from runtime type evidence.
Makes the result covariant and renderer contravariant, explaining both substitutions and forbidden positions.
Uses out and in projections for a copy boundary and explains star-projected reads and prohibited writes.
Allows erased classifier checks, rejects parameterized is-checks, and scopes any unchecked cast behind validation.
Explains reified limits and defers generated Java wildcard decisions to explicit interoperability design.

studyPaths.name: Kotlin and Java interoperability
studyPaths.description: Normalize Java uncertainty and deliberately design the JVM surface seen by Java clients and tooling.

scenario.title: Expose a predictable Kotlin API to Java and consume a Java API safely
scenario.context: A Kotlin order adapter reads an unannotated Java directory, accepts a Java callback, and publishes a facade used by a Java service and reflection-based framework. Treat the complete mixed-source examples in the lessons as the candidate API.

stages.prompt: Java lookup returns an unannotated String and sometimes null. Which Kotlin type should first hold it? What changes if the declaration uses Jakarta @Nullable under Kotlin 2.4?
stages.feedback: Use String? at the unannotated boundary and decide explicitly how to handle absence. Kotlin 2.4 reports a nullability mismatch as an error for jakarta.annotation.Nullable; an annotation improves static information but does not prove that a foreign implementation obeys its contract.
stages.nextConstraint: The directory also accepts a Java functional interface callback and exposes a JavaBean getter.

stages.prompt: Show the Kotlin lambda call and property-style access. Which Java members do those forms call, and what cannot be assumed about Java fields or Kotlin properties?
stages.feedback: A lambda can adapt to a Java SAM interface. directory.name is Kotlin syntax for a qualifying Java getName method; it invokes the method. A Kotlin property generally exposes accessors to Java, not a public field, and Java field access is not interchangeable with Kotlin property syntax.
stages.nextConstraint: The Kotlin facade needs a short Java call, stable static entry point, and catchable IOException.

stages.prompt: Choose @JvmStatic, @JvmOverloads, and @Throws where needed. State what Java sees with and without them, and name the binary/API compatibility cost.
stages.feedback: @JvmStatic exposes a companion method on the containing class; @JvmOverloads generates selected trailing-default overloads; @Throws declares IOException for Java checking. Java does not use Kotlin default-argument syntax. Generated overloads and JVM names are public signatures that need consumer tests and compatibility review.
stages.nextConstraint: The facade also accepts a covariant Kotlin producer and must be usable from Java.

stages.prompt: Predict the Java wildcard on a producer parameter, explain when @JvmSuppressWildcards changes it, and decide how to test the signature.
stages.feedback: Kotlin declaration-site out commonly maps to ? extends in a Java parameter position; return positions commonly omit the wildcard. @JvmSuppressWildcards removes it where chosen, which can narrow Java source compatibility. Compile a real Java caller and inspect signatures when reflection or a processor depends on them.
stages.nextConstraint: A framework scans getter and field annotations; a Java sealed result also enters the Kotlin adapter.

stages.prompt: Place the annotation on the Java element the framework scans, explain Kotlin 2.4 default targets and @all:, and handle a non-abstract Java sealed class in when.
stages.feedback: Use explicit @get:, @field:, or @param: for the required element, or @all: when supported propagation is intentional. Kotlin 2.4's stable default target rules can distribute annotations, so inspect compiled placement. For a non-abstract Java sealed class, Kotlin 2.4 requires a branch for the sealed class itself or else. Compile and run both consumption directions, then review source guarantees separately from emitted JVM metadata.
stages.nextConstraint: Before verification, a human checks pedagogy, official sources, interview realism, and version-specific wording.

debrief.connections: Platform types motivate boundary normalization; JavaBean access and SAM conversion simplify consumption; JVM annotations govern callable exposure; variance shapes Java wildcards; and annotation targets and sealed exhaustiveness affect frameworks and source compatibility.
debrief.tradeOffs: Kotlin syntax is concise, but a published cross-language library also commits to generated overloads, names, throws clauses, generic signatures, and annotation placement. Normalize uncertainty where it enters and compile real consumers before release.
rubric: Normalizes an unannotated Java return and explains Kotlin 2.4 Jakarta nullability enforcement.
Traces SAM and JavaBean conveniences to the underlying Java members.
Chooses static, overload, and throws exposure with a real Java caller.
Predicts variance-driven wildcards and validates the Java generic signature.
Places annotations for the actual scanner, handles Java sealed exhaustiveness, and distinguishes Kotlin source from JVM metadata.
